title: Split-horizon DNS + k8s network policy upgrade notes
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft: split-horizon DNS design + k8s network policy + NAT/firewall upgrade plan for on-prem / VPC-connected private deployments. Focus: minimize app impact during DNS/fwd changes, keep source-IP guarantees where required, and move TF modules to explicit versioned interfaces so upgrades can be rolled back quickly.

Context / motivation:
- Multiple customers run Redwood Private in customer datacenters or VPCs with mixed traffic patterns (internal services + customer-managed external endpoints).
- Current problems encountered: DNS hairpinning failures, inconsistent header preservation after NAT changes, overly-broad firewall rules, and k8s NetworkPolicy gaps after cluster upgrades.
- We need a repeatable TF-driven upgrade path that touches: private DNS zones (split-horizon), DNS forwarder config (CoreDNS/Bind), NAT gateway replacement (snat behavior), perimeter firewall rule tightening, and addition of Calico/K8s network policies for pod-level segmentation.

Scope (what this doc covers):
- Design notes: split-horizon DNS approach (zones + forwarders + TTLs)
- Terraform module interface suggestions for: private-dns-zone, dns-forwarders, nat-gateway, perimeter-firewall, k8s-network-policies
- Upgrade runbook (staging -> canary -> full roll) with smoke tests and rollback triggers
- Validation queries / metrics to watch
- Known risk areas and mitigations

High-level design decisions (draft):
1) Split-horizon: maintain two views for internal zone: internal.<customer-domain> and public.<customer-domain>. Internal view resolves private service IPs. Public view remains unchanged.
2) DNS forwarders: deploy regional forwarders that forward to on-prem resolvers for external names and to CoreDNS for internal zones. CoreDNS will host internal zones for Redwood-managed records.
3) TTL: set internal records TTL low during rollout (30s) to avoid caching surprises, raise to 300s after stabilization.
4) NAT: prefer stateful NAT appliances for egress where source-IP preservation is required. Provide optional SNAT pool mapping in TF module.
5) Firewall: move from wide allow lists to intent-based rulesets (named rule groups per app tier).
6) K8s NetworkPolicy: default deny at namespace level, explicit allow for known service-to-service flows. Use Calico globalNetworkPolicy for cross-namespace egress controls that must apply across CNI versions.

Terraform module notes (interface sketch):
- module "private_dns_zone":
    inputs: internal_zone_name (string), public_zone_name (string), forwarders (list of cidrs/ip), enable_split_horizon (bool), ttl (number)
    outputs: internal_zone_id, coredns_configmap_name

- module "dns_forwarders":
    inputs: forwarder_nics (list), forwarder_image (string), cluster_nodes (list), bind_options (map), healthcheck_port
    outputs: forwarder_ips, config_bucket_path

- module "nat_gateway":
    inputs: nat_type (appliance|cloud-nat), snat_pools (list of cidrs), preserve_src_ips (bool), ha (bool)
    outputs: nat_ips, route_table_id

- module "perimeter_firewall":
    inputs: allowed_ingress (list of {cidr,port,proto,name}), allowed_egress (list), admin_cidr_whitelist, audit_logging (bool)
    outputs: fw_policy_id, ruleset_version

- module "k8s_network_policies":
    inputs: namespace (string), default_deny (bool), policy_rules (list of maps with from/to/ports/protocols), enforcement_mode (Enforce|Monitor)
    outputs: policy_names, audit_report_location

Implementation tips / gotchas:
- CoreDNS: when switching views, watch for cached negative responses on resolvers upstream; negative TTLs can cause long-lived failures. Use short TTLs and staged promotion.
- Hairpin/NAT: some on-prem switches drop hairpinned traffic when SNAT is in place. Test pod->node->service hairpin behavior in staging cluster.
- Source IP preservation: if application depends on client IP, ensure either proxy inserts X-Forwarded-For or preserve source using non-SNAT routing + proxy. Document services that rely on source IP.
- Firewall change windows: coordinate with customer ops; tightening rules often triggers support tickets. Include a fallback period of 48h where we revert to old rules if >3 escalations.
- TF state: plan a migration strategy for state names when renaming modules - keep old resources untouched until new module fully validated. Use separate workspaces for canary clusters.

Upgrade rollout plan (step-by-step):
Phase 0 — Discovery (1–2 days)
- Inventory current DNS zones and forwarders (dig + zone transfer where allowed).
- Map services that require source-IP (auth, licensing, audit).
- Record firewall rules (export to CSV).
- Create JIRA epic: JIRA-INFRA-2043 (see linked_artifacts).

Phase 1 — Staging (2–4 days)
- Deploy TF modules to staging workspace (private-dns, forwarders, nat-gateway stubbed, firewall restrict with monitor only).
- Configure CoreDNS with split-horizon internal zone; set TTL=30s.
- Run smoke tests: curl internal services via internal name, dig internal zone from client node and from external node.
- Observe: DNS latency, failed lookups, pod egress connections.

Phase 2 — Canary (1–3 days)
- Enable changes for a single cluster and a small set of namespaces (10% of traffic).
- Deploy k8s-network-policies with enforcement_mode=Monitor first, gather deny logs.
- Switch NAT mode for canary cluster using nat-gateway module with preserve_src_ips as appropriate.
- Monitor: 5xx error rate, DNS NXDOMAINs, increased DNS latency, broken inbound flows.

Phase 3 — Gradual roll (3–7 days)
- Expand to remaining clusters in waves (25% -> 50% -> 100%).
- After each wave: increase internal TTL 30s -> 120s -> 300s once stable for 24h.

Phase 4 — Hardening and cleanup
- Remove monitor-only network policies and enable enforcement.
- Rotate configs: remove temporary forwarders and consolidate.
- Bump TF module versions and tag releases.

Rollback criteria and triggers:
- If applicant traffic error rate > 2x baseline for >30m and not explained by transient load spikes -> rollback.
- More than 5 distinct customer escalations in 24h.
- Lost ability to reach critical internal control-plane endpoints (etcd, k8s API).
Rollback steps:
- Revert TF workspace to previous module version and apply in reverse order (firewall back to old rules, NAT back to old appliance, DNS view revert).
- Immediately raise TTLs for internal zone to 600s to reduce DNS churn if DNS instability is due to churn (note this slows recovery after rollback).
- Open incident in PagerDuty, notify customers via status channel.

Smoke tests and commands (examples):
- dig @<forwarder_ip> service.internal.customer.example +short
- dig +trace internal.customer.example
- curl --resolve "service.internal.customer.example:443:<internal_ip>" https://service.internal.customer.example/health -v
- kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -sS http://service.namespace.svc.cluster.local/health
- iptables-save | grep <nat_ip> (verify SNAT rules on node where NAT is managed)

Metrics & dashboards to watch: (must be in Redwood Console / Prometheus)
- DNS: queries/sec, error_rate (NXDOMAIN/REFUSED), latency p95/p99 to forwarders
- TCP/HTTP: 5xx rate, latency p95 for affected services
- NAT: SNAT sessions usage, port exhaustion alerts
- Firewall: dropped_packets by rule, audit logging volume
- NetworkPolicy: denied connections (for monitor->enforce tuning)

Testing matrix (recommended):
- Vendor switch types: test hairpin on Broadcom, Mellanox, and Cisco variants in staging.
- CNI versions: Calico v3.x vs v4.x behavior with globalNetworkPolicy
- k8s patch versions that might affect kube-proxy mode (iptables vs ipvs)
- TLS termination differences when preserving source IP vs SNAT

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we publish a canonical customer-facing KB about expected maintenance windows for firewall changes? (TODO @Priya)
- Should we support a fully-managed DNS appliance option for customers that cannot run CoreDNS? (decide by 2025-01-31)
- Validate behavior of service-mesh sidecars (Istio) when source IP is changed by NAT. Add tests. (assigned Miguel)

Appendix: example CoreDNS internal zone ConfigMap snippet (draft)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns-custom
data:
  Corefile: |
    internal.customer.example:53 {
      file /etc/coredns/zones/internal.customer.example.db
      ttl 30
      errors
      log
    }

Appendix: minimal TF var examples (yaml-like for readability)
- private_dns.tfvars:
  internal_zone_name = "internal.customer.example"
  public_zone_name = "customer.example"
  forwarders = ["10.20.0.5","10.20.0.6"]
  enable_split_horizon = true
  ttl = 30

- nat.tfvars:
  nat_type = "appliance"
  preserve_src_ips = true
  snat_pools = ["198.51.100.0/28"]

Contacts / escalation:
- primary: Daniel Kim (owner) - slack: @daniel.kim, pager: oncall-sre
- secondary: Priya Shah - slack: @priyash

Notes (freeform):
- Keep playbook short and prescriptive; link to longer Confluence designs for deep-dive.
- This doc intentionally mixes higher-level runbook steps with TF interface sketches to help engineers implement without flipping between many pages.
- When converting monitor-only policies to enforce, expect a cleanup week where we tune policies and add service exceptions.
